task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper reported feature for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of June 16, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: The Materials Recovery Lab at Westfield University has developed a rare earth extraction process that recovers neodymium and dysprosium from discarded electric vehicle motors at 78% efficiency.
Virgin ore processing achieves roughly 90% recovery; the 12-percentage-point gap is the primary technical barrier the lab is working to close.

Lab director Dr. Priya Sundaram said the process uses an ionic liquid solvent that selectively dissolves rare earth elements from the magnet matrix without the high-temperature roasting required in conventional processing.
Sundaram said: "The chemistry is not new. What we've done is make it scalable at room temperature. That changes the energy economics substantially."
Graduate student Tomás Vargas, 27, has spent three years optimizing the solvent regeneration cycle — the step that allows the ionic liquid to be reused rather than discarded after each batch.

Vargas said the first attempts failed because the solvent gradually absorbed impurities from the magnet alloy that degraded its selectivity; the team tested 14 regeneration approaches before finding one that restored 96% of the original selectivity.
Vargas said: "Science is the fourteen failures. The paper is the one success. The fourteen failures took three years."
The lab processes approximately 200 kilograms of magnet material per week in its current pilot configuration; a commercial-scale version would need to process tons per day.
Westfield's technology licensing office is in discussions with two undisclosed industrial partners about pilot plant investment; no agreement has been signed.
Sundaram said the source material problem is currently the binding constraint: there are not yet enough end-of-life EV motors available in concentrated enough volumes to supply a commercial facility.
Most EV motors in service were built after 2017; with typical vehicle lifetimes of 12 to 15 years, large volumes of end-of-life motors will begin entering the waste stream around 2030 to 2032.

A Department of Energy report estimated that if 50% of rare earths in end-of-life EV motors were recovered by 2040, recycling could supply 15% of projected U.S. demand for neodymium — a significant but not transformative contribution.

The economics of rare earth recycling are highly sensitive to primary market prices; when rare earth oxide prices fall, the recycling margin disappears; when prices are high, the process becomes profitable.
Sundaram said she is designing the process to be profitable at the current market price of $65 per kilogram for neodymium oxide; the process needs to be viable at $50 to be commercially robust.
Two automotive companies have pledged to send decommissioned vehicle test units to the lab to maintain a feedstock supply during the pilot phase.

Vargas plans to defend his dissertation in 2025 and has accepted a research position at a company developing urban mining processes; he said the lab's work convinced him that chemistry can be a supply chain tool.

Sundaram said the rare earth recycling field is currently populated by small startups with limited capital; the technology needs industrial partners with existing chemical processing infrastructure to scale.

Dr. Sundaram said the most important outcome of the lab's work may not be the specific process: it is demonstrating that room-temperature ionic liquid approaches are viable, which other researchers can build on.

Vargas said his primary motivation was supply chain security, not environmental impact: "If rare earths are a national security issue, then recycling them is a national security project. That's how I think about the three years."

Sundaram noted that her lab's process produces less wastewater and no radioactive byproduct streams, unlike primary ore processing, which must manage thorium and uranium co-extracted with rare earths.
